Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson says that despite Apple's claims of vetting submissions, blatant rating fraud continues to slip through the App Store.

He says he wasn't intentionally searching for scam apps on the App Store, but keeps stumbling across them, and shared a recent example...

The App Store is a "safe and trusted place"

Apple takes a hard line on any antitrust measures involving third-party App Stores or iPhone sideloading, often only giving ground when legally compelled. Even so, Apple continues to argue its case.

The company claims this isn't about money, but about protecting iPhone users from malware. For example, Apple said last year that it had blocked over $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

Many developers, however, question the claim that the App Store is a safe place, pointing to numerous scams involving millions of dollars. Just last month, Apple was sued by three customers who said their Bitcoin was entirely stolen by a fake wallet app.

App Store rating fraud

App Store rating fraud is a long-standing problem, with some companies even renting out "iPhone farms" in mainland China to mass-download apps and leave five-star reviews.

Developer Jeff Johnson (best known for his StopTheMadness Safari extension) says he considers this latest case of App Store review fraud to be "massive and obvious." The app in question is TabControl Extension.

He says when he stumbled across the app, it was ranked 12th on the US Mac App Store chart for paid Safari extensions, with screenshots that were clearly AI-generated fake images.

Another thing worth noting is that the fake screenshots claim the app is rated "4.9 out of 5 stars," misleading people into thinking these are App Store user reviews... Using App Store screenshots to make false claims is a common scam tactic I've mentioned before. When a developer submits an app to the App Store, Apple reviews not only the app itself but also the App Store listing data and metadata, including screenshots. The claims in scam app screenshots are often absurd to the extreme, yet Apple still approves them... Apple claims the App Store protects users from dishonest developers. If App Store review can't even catch this kind of thing, what's the point of having a review? In fact, App Store review doesn't need to be as thorough as mine. A screenshot claiming "4.9 out of 5 stars" is itself a red flag. Apple has records of all ratings and reviews in every country, so they know full well this is false advertising. I don't even need to download the damn app to know the developer is trying to scam users.

As he puts it, if a developer is willing to use deceptive tactics to promote their app from the start, you certainly wouldn't want to hand over your browsing data to them.

9to5Mac's take

Of course, eliminating all App Store scams entirely is impossible, but fake reviews are extremely common, and a case like this should have been obvious to Apple. How on earth this extension passed review is baffling.

Apple should at least put a mechanism in place to automatically subject any app climbing the charts to more rigorous review, examining both the app itself and the claims it makes.
